analyst_fiscal_rows.label: Employee and self-employed social contributions change
Employer social contributions change
analyst_fiscal_rows.gloss: Simulated from a contract class this build derives by proxy, and the proxy is ours rather than EUROMOD's. Every one of the seven Italian employer-contribution components is gated on the blue or white-collar class, whose documented construction uses a national IT-SILC variable the public EU-SILC user database does not carry. The contract class is derived from occupation, which the codebook does publish for Italy, by treating ISCO-08 major groups 6 to 9 as blue collar and 0 to 5 as white, over everyone with employment income, with EUROMOD's own default of blue collar where no occupation is recorded. No EUROMOD country derives the class from occupation, so this rule is not the model author's. It gives a baseline of EUR 181,054m, against EUROMOD's own published 2023 baseline of EUR 179,797m, the EUR 180,821m of employer contributions EU-SILC itself records, and an external EUR 204,586m (EUROMOD Italy country report Y16_CR_IT, table A3.6). It sits inside the bracket the class can produce at all, EUR 177,906m if every employee were white collar and EUR 191,133m if every one were blue. It is still a proxy: it puts 22 per cent of employees in blue collar against a national share nearer half, and because sickness and maternity is the only rate that differs between the classes, the whole of that error falls on that one component. The case for the convention is not that it is principled but that it is checked: it lands within 1 per cent of two figures that were not used to build it, EUROMOD's own published baseline and the employer contributions EU-SILC records independently, and inside a bracket whose ends are 7 per cent apart with the published baseline between them. A rule chosen to fit would have had one such check, not two.

scenario_extra.statement: The AdI uplift costs {{SPINE_COST_A}} and the IRPEF cut costs {{SPINE_COST_B}}. They are not the same size: about {{SPINE_GAP_PCT}} per cent apart, with {{SPINE_CHEAPER}} the cheaper of the two. Two reforms of different size cannot be compared on their absolute welfare effects, because the larger one moves more money and so scores higher at ε=0 whatever its targeting. The comparison here is therefore per euro of exchequer cost. On that measure the two are exactly equally efficient at ε=0, where the welfare measure is simply the money moved: 1.000 against 1.000. As ε rises the bottom-targeted transfer pulls ahead, reaching 1.626 against 0.900 at ε=1 and 2.660 against 0.945 at ε=2, because a euro reaching a poorer household counts for more while the tax cut's value falls away. The same pattern holds in all three EU tools. It is a statement about ratios, not about which reform is larger, and the per-euro columns of the table below are where to read it. (The AdI effect is large partly because base-amount scaling also brings newly-eligible households into the scheme, so this dial is not the same experiment as Spain's or Greece's.)

ui.single_note: Single-reform explorer. Exactly one control is active at a time: moving any slider resets the others to baseline. Combinations are not supported: the response surface is built from single-reform grids, which cannot represent how two reforms interact. Italy has no binary toggle.
ui.epsnote: ε = inequality aversion. 0 = every € counts equally; 1 = a € to a household at or below the poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much; 2 = about 2.8 times. Those are the maxima: living standards are floored at 60% of the median before the weight is taken. ε is a value judgement you set. See the Home tab for detail.
ui.welfare_measure: What this measures: the euro value of the reform's effect on household welfare, where a euro of gain to a poorer household counts for more than the same euro to a richer one (ε sets how much more). It is distributionally weighted euros, not simply the total euros gained. Shown in 2024 euros (×1.0197).
ui.scenarios_epsnote: ε = inequality aversion. 0 = every € counts equally; 1 = a € to a household at or below the poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much; 2 = about 2.8 times. Those are the maxima: living standards are floored at 60% of the median before the weight is taken. The scenario ranking reorders as ε rises.

unemployment_caveat: The exchequer cost of the unemployment scenarios EXCLUDES the contributory unemployment-benefit response and therefore UNDERSTATES the true fiscal cost: the model's les-flip mechanism removes earnings but does not confer unemployment-benefit eligibility.
capacity_caveat: The capacity and shock model is INDICATIVE: it uses UK-derived operational parameters (demand elasticities and staff ratios), scaled to this country's own {{UNITS}} but not Italy-calibrated. The shock magnitudes are computed points on this country's own surface, but the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner is the UK's own share, applied to this country's own WORKING-AGE unit count so that the base matches the one the UK measures the share on. Treat the demand, utilisation and gap figures as order-of-magnitude, not a local forecast.
provenance: EU-SILC 2024 wave; income reference year 2023; EUROMOD policy system 2023 (IT_2023). Analyst welfare, distributional and fiscal results come from the validated response surface (the fiscal figures are its re-emitted net exchequer cost). Analyst monetary values are 2023 nominal EUR shown in 2024 EUR (×1.0197, Eurostat nama_10_gdp B1GQ PD15_NAC); Provider values are 2024-equivalent EUR. The minimum-income dial models take-up entry (newly-eligible households), not strictly comparable to ES/EL. Built on the EU-SILC data, run through EUROMOD rather than EUROMOD's own bundled input dataset (the EMSD), which applies EUROMOD's own harmonisation and imputation; welfare and distributional results are validated against the EUROMOD Country-Report baseline, and the effect on fiscal levels of running EU-SILC directly rather than the EMSD is unquantified (neither equivalent to a standard EUROMOD run nor inferior, only prepared differently). The conversion populates 44 input columns. Italy's derivable set is small because 49 of the variables its model reads and this build leaves empty have recipes that name a national IT-SILC variable, including both unemployment components, the child and maternity components, and the cadastral values. The contract class is derived from occupation by a proxy of ours, and every Italian employer-contribution component depends on it. Aggregates only; no microdata.
home_html:
About the project

BENEFITS develops a Holistic Appraisal Framework (HAF) to measure the social, economic and environmental value-added of social services. HAF combines real household microdata and tax-benefit microsimulation with “beyond GDP” valuation methods to quantify how policy reforms and social services affect people's welfare. Findings are consolidated through a Social Services Policy Observatory and citizen assemblies, supported by a Visualisations Platform, and built into a Policy Evaluation Toolkit to inform policymaking.

Full title: Building Economic, Needs-Based and Environmental evaluation Frameworks for Inclusive Transformation of Social services in Europe. Coordinator: KMOP, with 10 partners across 7 countries. Funding: Horizon Europe, grant agreement no. 101179032.

About this tool

This is the Italian edition of the Microsimulation Valuation Tool. It lets you move each reform family continuously across its modelled range and read the distributional welfare, fiscal, and provider responses for Italy. It reads a pre-computed response surface ({{POINTS_PER_DIAL}}, each already passed through the welfare layer, computed on EUROMOD IT_2023 over the EU-SILC 2024 wave) and interpolates linearly between those points as you drag a slider. It does not run the tax-benefit engine live using microdata, and ships only aggregate welfare, distributional and fiscal results, no microdata. All monetary values are in 2024 euros: 2023 nominal values uprated by the Italian GDP deflator, ×1.0197.

⚠ Minimum-income note. Italy's Assegno di Inclusione dial scales the base amount, which models both a higher payment and newly-eligible households entering the scheme (take-up entry). This is genuinely different from Greece's and Spain's existing-recipient top-up, and makes Italy's minimum-income effects larger and not strictly comparable across countries.

The {{DIAL_COUNT}} dials

  • Minimum income (AdI, Assegno di Inclusione): increases the base amount by 0 to +50%, from a base of about €6,000 a year. Scaling the base models both a higher payment and newly-eligible households entering the scheme.
  • Universal child benefit (AUU, Assegno Unico Universale): increases the allowance by 0 to +50%. The maximum is about €189.18 a month per child.
  • Personal Income Tax (IRPEF, Imposta sul Reddito delle Persone Fisiche) first-bracket rate: changes the 23% rate on income up to €15,000 across the modelled range, from a 5 percentage point (pp) cut to a 5pp rise. This is a rate change, not a change to the tax-free allowance.
  • Earnings downturn (market income): reduces market income by 0 to 10%, a direct earnings cut, not job losses.
  • Unemployment shock: raises unemployment by 0 to 10pp, modelled as that share of employed people losing their earnings.

One reform at a time

The tool enforces single-reform exploration: exactly one control is active at any moment, and moving any control resets the others to baseline. The response surface is calculated one reform at a time; combining two reforms is not the sum of their separate effects, because reforms interact, so the tool will not show a number it cannot stand behind.

Inequality aversion (ε)

ε sets how much more a €1 welfare gain to a lower-income household counts than the same €1 to a higher-income household. It is a value judgement you choose, not a result the tool dictates; as you change ε, the welfare figure updates to reflect it.

  • ε = 0: every €1 counts equally, regardless of income (pure efficiency; the utilitarian case).
  • ε = 1: the standard central value, a €1 gain to a household at or below the at-risk-of-poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much as the same €1 to a household on the median.
  • ε = 2: strong inequality aversion, the same gain counts about 2.8 times. That is the maximum: the living standard is floored at the at-risk-of-poverty line (AROP), 60% of the median, before the weight is taken.

A bottom-targeted reform, such as a higher minimum income guarantee, grows more valuable as ε rises; a reform whose gains sit higher up the distribution, such as a tax rate cut, shrinks as ε rises.

How to use it

Analyst mode. Set ε, then move one dial and read the results: the welfare effect, the ε strip (how that effect changes across ε values), the fiscal cost, the winners-and-losers split, and the decile chart. The other controls snap back to baseline whenever you move one.

Provider mode. Enter a caseload and targeting profile, then read the value ladder (defined below). Every value shown includes its source and provenance. The capacity-gap and shock views are indicative only. Their demand elasticities and staff ratios are registry assumptions rather than measured national figures, and the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner is the UK's own share applied to this country's WORKING-AGE unit count, matching the base the UK measures that share on, so only that base is local.

The value ladder, a stepped set of value estimates, from the most conservative at the bottom to the fullest at the top:

  • Cash floor: the value counting only the direct cash the service moves (benefits paid or income secured). A deliberately conservative lower bound.
  • Headline: the cash floor plus the monetised value of the service's wider social outcomes, for example wellbeing gains. The main figure to quote.
  • Low/central/high band: the range around the headline, reflecting genuine uncertainty in those social-outcome values.

Scenarios mode. {{SCENARIO_COUNT_CAP}} fixed reforms and shocks, each with its fiscal cost, distributional effect, welfare, and cost-effectiveness, plus the spine, which compares the minimum income uplift with the tax cut per euro of exchequer cost rather than on their absolute effects, because the two reforms are not the same size. Per euro they are exactly equally efficient at ε = 0, where the welfare measure is just the money moved, and the uplift pulls ahead as ε rises.

Data year: EU-SILC 2024 wave; income reference year 2023; EUROMOD policy system IT_2023. Built on the EU-SILC data (2024 wave), run through EUROMOD - not EUROMOD's own bundled input dataset (the EMSD), which prepares its inputs with EUROMOD's own harmonisation and imputation. The welfare and distributional results are validated against the EUROMOD Country-Report baseline; the effect of this input difference on the fiscal figures is not quantified. Aggregates only; no microdata.

gdp_shock.label: Earnings downturn (market income)
gdp_shock.base: Market income (employees' and self-employed earnings, yem/yse, plus yseev for Italy) is scaled down by the shown percentage; baseline is 0%. This is an across-the-board earnings cut for people in work, not job losses.
gdp_shock.explain: An earnings downturn lowers households' incomes and the income tax and social-insurance contributions they pay, which is why it costs the exchequer (lost revenue) even though few extra benefits are triggered.
gdp_shock.winlose: Working households across the distribution lose a little earnings; the near-zero winners share is low-income households whose means-tested support rises slightly as earnings fall.

pit_give.label: IRPEF first-bracket rate change
pit_give.base: Italy's personal income tax (IRPEF) first-bracket rate is 23% (on income up to €15,000; the tintsna_rate1 constant, group 9). Baseline is 0 pp. The dial cuts this rate by the shown percentage points. A tax-free-allowance dial is not offered because no single such constant is exposed in the model, so the lever is a rate cut.
pit_give.explain: Cutting the IRPEF first-bracket rate returns money to income-tax payers, who sit in the middle and upper parts of the distribution, so its welfare value falls as the weight on poorer households (ε) rises.
pit_give.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers in the middle and upper-middle deciles; the poorest gain little because they pay little income tax. There are no losers.

child_benefit_up.label: Universal child benefit (AUU, Assegno Unico Universale)
child_benefit_up.base: Italy's Assegno Unico Universale (AUU), the near-universal child benefit, with a maximum of about €189.18 per month per child (ISEE-banded). Baseline is 0%; the dial raises the AUU amounts by the shown percentage (an in-memory scaling of the BenCalc schedule; the realised rise is approximately the shown percentage, concentrated in the flat and maximum bands).
child_benefit_up.explain: Raising the AUU helps families with children across the income range (it is near-universal), so the gain is broad; its welfare value holds up moderately as ε rises.
child_benefit_up.winlose: Winners are families with children across the distribution; there are no losers.

min_income_up.label: Assegno di Inclusione: higher payment and newly-eligible entry
min_income_up.base: Italy's AdI minimum income, base amount about €6,000 a year. AdI is the instrument code used throughout this project; the scheme name we attach to it is Assegno di Inclusione, and that name is ours, not the model's. What the model supplies is the instrument bsamm_s and the constant $bsa_Amount1 that this dial scales, in system IT_2023. Baseline is 0%. The dial scales the base amount by the shown percentage. NOTE: Italy's minimum income moves by base-amount scaling, which models BOTH a higher payment to existing recipients AND newly-eligible households ENTERING the scheme (take-up entry) - genuinely different from Greece's and Spain's existing-recipient top-up, and its welfare and fiscal effects are correspondingly larger.
min_income_up.explain: A higher AdI base amount is a transfer to low-income households; because it also brings newly-eligible households into the scheme, its welfare value is large and grows as the weight on poorer households (ε) rises. NOTE: Italy's minimum income moves by base-amount scaling, which models BOTH a higher payment to existing recipients AND newly-eligible households ENTERING the scheme (take-up entry) - genuinely different from Greece's and Spain's existing-recipient top-up, and its welfare and fiscal effects are correspondingly larger.
min_income_up.winlose: Winners are low-income households, both existing recipients and newly-eligible entrants; there are no losers, because the uplift is funded from general taxation. NOTE: Italy's minimum income moves by base-amount scaling, which models BOTH a higher payment to existing recipients AND newly-eligible households ENTERING the scheme (take-up entry) - genuinely different from Greece's and Spain's existing-recipient top-up, and its welfare and fiscal effects are correspondingly larger.

unemployment_shock.label: Unemployment shock
unemployment_shock.base: Baseline is 0 pp. The dial raises unemployment by the shown percentage points, modelled as that share of employed people losing their earnings (a nested les-flip for monotonicity).
unemployment_shock.explain: A rise in unemployment removes earnings from the people who lose their jobs. NOTE: the modelled fiscal cost excludes the contributory unemployment-benefit response and therefore understates the true cost.
unemployment_shock.winlose: Losers are the households pushed out of work; the small winners share is households the benefit system more than compensates for a modest earnings loss. The exchequer cost shown excludes the contributory unemployment-benefit response.

profiles_provenance_note: Targeting bands defined as decile groups (1 to 3, 4 to 6, and all ten). A presentational choice about which part of the distribution a service serves, with no source; the user selects among them.

services.name: Employment support
services.flag: Closest available estimate: 0.46 WELLBY at the €14,925 spine (HM Treasury Wellbeing Guidance 2021: £13,000 at 2019 prices, uprated and PPP-adjusted to Italy); transferred from the UK Britain fixed-effects unemployment-to-employment coefficient as no Italian figure exists. That gives €6,866 for one person moving into work, within a €5,282 to €8,452 band. THAT IS NOT THE VALUE THIS TOOL APPLIES: it is the wellbeing figure before the two valuation stages. The tool applies €453 per person re-employed, within a €116 to €1050 band, being that figure times an effect share of 0.30 (0.11 low, 0.46 high) and an attribution of 0.22 (0.20 low, 0.27 high). Both quantities are per person re-employed, which is why the smaller one is named here: quoting €6,866 as the value overstates it about fifteenfold. The stages, their sources and every denominator are on the value's own note.

Italy holds a per-capita SERT cost of its own, EMCDDA Insights 24 (2017), chapter 7, the Bergamo case study, table 7.8, which at 2024 is EUR 4,463.3 excluding inpatient care on the 2013 base and EUR 4,720.5 on the 2014 base, or EUR 32,084.1 and EUR 31,408.0 including it. Three reasons, and any one of them is sufficient. IT IS NOT NATIONAL: it is one city's service, Bergamo, carried in the source as a case study, so adopting it would read a local observation as an Italian unit cost. IT IS NOT THE SAME QUANTITY: it is whole-service expenditure per client of a SERT, which covers clients and activities this row does not, against a per-case cost of delivering opioid substitution. AND ITS SCOPE IS UNRESOLVED: the two variants differ by a factor of about seven, EUR 4,463.3 against EUR 32,084.1, on nothing more than whether inpatient care is counted, and nothing in this tree chooses between them. Adopting either would also break the one-concept-per-row discipline that lets the Spanish, Italian and Greek cells be read beside each other, since the other two would stay on an ex-medication delivery cost. Employment support.provenance_note: 0.46 WELLBY transferred from the UK Britain fixed-effects coefficient (Clark et al. 2018), valued on this country's PPP-adjusted spine, then staged. Transfer with a stated adjustment. ORIGIN 16300 FACTOR 0.42120360; BAND ORIGIN 12540 AND 20064; STAGE EFFECT 0.11 0.30 0.46 ATTRIBUTION 0.20 0.22 0.27. The origin is the UK WELLBY spine at 2024 prices and its low and high tiers; the factor is the household-final-consumption PPP to Italy, 0.915660, times the 0.46 coefficient. The stages apply in all four tools. An attribution share is the tool's convention rather than a national fact, so it needs no national warrant; the effect share is an empirical value borrowed between countries and is flagged as such below. EFFECT SHARE, an OUTCOME RATE, and a BORROWED one: 0.30 central from the Work and Health Programme job-outcome rate of 31 per cent and the Restart Scheme rate of 30 per cent, 0.11 low from Additional Work Coach Support, 0.46 high from the Work and Health Programme first-earnings rate. These are BRITISH PROGRAMME RATES APPLIED WITHOUT NATIONAL ADJUSTMENT, on a denominator of programme starts. No equivalent national rate exists for this country, and the national active labour market policy evidence is carried as a qualitative warrant only, with no effect size, by the project's own standing rule. ATTRIBUTION, an IMPACT: 0.22 central within a sourced range of 0.20, the Department for Work and Pensions' own Restart additionality projection of six in a hundred over the thirty in a hundred reaching a job outcome THE SIX IN A HUNDRED IS THE DEPARTMENT'S OWN BUSINESS-CASE PROJECTION AND NOT A STATISTICAL FINDING. It is published in House of Commons Committee of Public Accounts, The Restart Scheme for Long-term Unemployed People, Forty-Second Report of Session 2022-23, HC 733, 22 March 2023, at Conclusions and recommendations paragraph 1, where the committee quotes the Department's expectation of a return of 2.44 pounds for every pound spent and its estimate that an extra six in a hundred participants will find sustained work above what would have happened anyway, and warns in the same sentence that if that estimate is too high the benefits of the scheme will quickly fall away. The committee measured nothing here; it is reporting what the Department expected., and 0.27, the three-percentage-point Additional Work Coach Support impact over its eleven per cent in-work rate. THE PUBLICATION IS Department for Work and Pensions, The impact of additional Jobcentre Plus support on the employment outcomes of disabled people, research and analysis, 18 March 2025, which states that twelve months after the intervention 11 per cent of participants were in work compared to 8 per cent of the comparison group, a 3 percentage point employment impact, and that the impact is statistically significant. It is NOT the qualitative report The experience of Additional Work Coach Support of 2 May 2025, which carries no percentage at all and refers the reader to this impact analysis. A LATER PUBLICATION RESTATES THE SAME TWELVE-MONTH COMPARISON AND THIS VALUE DOES NOT FOLLOW IT: the extended impact assessment at 24 months, Official Statistics, 25 March 2026, gives 11 per cent against 8.2 per cent, an impact of 2.8 percentage points, which on the same arithmetic would put this bound at 2.8 over 11 = 0.2545 rather than 0.2727. The shipped 0.27 is the March 2025 figure and is unchanged; the restatement is recorded here so the difference is accounted for rather than left for a reader to find. The effect share's low bound of 0.11 is unaffected, because both publications put the participant rate at 11 per cent. The full derivation and every denominator are on the United Kingdom cell. meta.note: IT Analyst response surface. Single-reform magnitude grids; one lever per point; baseline is the zero point of each dial. WEVM and decile contributions in EUR MILLIONS, equivalised, median-anchored, AROP-floored. Native 2023 income reference year (EU-SILC 2024 wave); nominal EUR, no uprating, no PPP (downstream). units.fiscal: EUR millions versus baseline; net_exchequer_cost_m = benefit - tax - sic - sic_employer, positive is a cost to the exchequer

meta.poverty_basis: Two thresholds, both emitted at every point. RELATIVE (relative_*): 60% of that point's own weighted median equivalised (OECD-modified) household disposable income, the published AROP convention and the same line the social weight uses as its floor; it moves with the reform, so a reform that lowers the median lowers the line and can cut the measured count without raising anyone's income. ANCHORED (anchored_*): the same 60%-of-median line computed once at the zero-magnitude baseline point and held fixed across every point of every dial, emitted as anchored_bhc_threshold_cur so it is auditable; internally defined, needing no external source, and the right comparison of a reform against its own baseline. ANCHORED IS NOT ABSOLUTE: the absolute_* fields mean a fixed EXTERNAL base year and stay null because no sourced one exists for ES, IT or EL. The AHC fields are null throughout because the EUROMOD per-unit layer carries no housing-cost concept. All other field names follow the UK surface exactly.
meta.rebuild: Built on EUROMOD v3.8.6, on a COMPLETED input conversion. Every input variable a live 2023 policy reads, for which the EUROMOD input data codebook publishes a recipe and whose sources the public EU-SILC user database carries, is populated from that recipe: Spain carries 68 populated input columns, Greece 55, Italy 44. The consequential ones are Spain's pension and unemployment decompositions and its rent, mortgage and private-pension deductions; Greece's property tax, which is the ENFIA the model reads and passes through; and Italy's contract class, without which no employer contribution fires at all. A surface is a function of its inputs, so reproducing a stored surface is not the test; the test is agreement with each country's own published EUROMOD baseline, recorded in europe/docs/BASELINE_VALIDATION.md. Conventions this surface holds: the stable sort in build_grid.point_from_pu and in wevm._weighted_median / wevm.wevm_by_decile, the two-sided pit_give grid, and the fiscal and poverty objects emitted in the same pass, fiscal by the method of re_emit.py. Poverty carries both a relative (moving) and an anchored (held at baseline) threshold; see poverty_basis.

min_income_up.short: This dial's cost is OVERSTATED. The outlay is about 11 per cent above the model's own figure and about a third above the published spend.
min_income_up.detail: This dial's means test applies its second-property asset test. The ISEE reads the cadastral value of the household's property, and this build derives the value of buildings other than the main residence by inverting the property tax the survey records at the statutory revaluation the model itself uses, giving EUR 9,784m against the EUR 9,245m the country report publishes for that variable. The modelled outlay is EUR 8,854m, against EUROMOD's own EUR 7,971m and an external EUR 6,653m (Italy country report Y16_CR_IT, table A3.6), so it remains overstated by about 11 per cent against the model's own figure and by about a third against the published spend. The main-residence component of the ISEE is still missing and it is the larger of the two: the same table values it at EUR 12,792m of cadastral income against EUR 9,245m for other buildings. There is no route to it, because the property tax exempts the main residence and there is nothing to invert.

child_benefit_up.short: This dial's cost is OVERSTATED and its incidence is not flat. The baseline it scales is about 9 per cent above the model's own figure and 16 per cent above the published spend.
child_benefit_up.detail: This dial's cost is OVERSTATED and its incidence is not flat. The Assegno Unico is banded on a means-tested income the model derives from the ISEE, and this build supplies the ISEE's second-property component, derived by inverting the property tax the survey records at the statutory revaluation the model itself uses. The baseline this dial scales is EUR 20,235m against EUROMOD's own EUR 18,538m and an external EUR 17,382m (Italy country report Y16_CR_IT, table A3.6), so about 9 per cent above the model's own figure and 16 per cent above the published spend. Measured on the variable the model actually bands on, 47 per cent of recipients and 61 per cent of the outlay sit in the maximum-amount band, 42 per cent in the taper and 11 per cent at the minimum. The ISEE's main-residence component is still missing, which is why the overstatement has not gone: the same table values it at EUR 12,792m of cadastral income against EUR 9,245m for the second-property component this build supplies.

pit_give.short: This dial reaches more people than the real schedule does, because the variable selecting Italy's flat-tax regime is absent and is zero for everyone. It overstates its own effect by 12 to 13 per cent at the statutory bound and by roughly 3 per cent at the number of electors Italy records.
pit_give.detail: This dial reaches more people than the real schedule does. It changes the first IRPEF bracket rate, and in this build every self-employed person is inside that schedule, because the variable that selects Italy's 15 per cent flat-tax regime is a national imputation the public EU-SILC user database does not carry and is therefore zero for everyone. In reality about 1.9 million taxpayers were in that regime in 2023, and a rate change to the progressive schedule does not reach them. Measured on this build: if everyone statutorily eligible were in the regime, the dial's income tax effect at minus 2 percentage points would fall from EUR 10,210m to between EUR 9,099m and EUR 9,036m, so the dial overstates its own effect by 12 to 13 per cent at that bound, and by roughly 3 per cent at the number of electors Italy actually records. The direction is certain and the size is a range, so no corrected figure is shown.

gdp_shock.short: The contributions figures here include a self-employed leg 93.8 per cent above its published level (EUR 39,037m against EUR 20,144m). It accounts for roughly 3 to 4 per cent of the net cost shown.
gdp_shock.detail: The contributions figures on this dial contain a self-employed leg 93.8 per cent above the amount the country report publishes: EUR 39,037m against EUR 20,144m, and against an external EUR 20,716m. The published amount is table A3.4; table A3.3 gives Number of payers (thousands) and is not an amount. The row labelled employee and self-employed social contributions is ils_sicdy, which is both legs plus other contributions; the self-employed leg is 48 per cent of it at baseline, 34 to 36 per cent of the change on this earnings downturn and 44 to 49 per cent on the unemployment shock. Taking the part attributable to the divergence alone, it is 2.9 to 3.0 per cent of the displayed net exchequer cost on the earnings downturn and 3.5 to 3.9 per cent on the unemployment shock. That is a proportional attribution, not a re-simulation: it says what the change would have been had the contribution base been at its published level and responded in the same proportion. No correction has been applied. The cause is a contribution-base concept the public EU-SILC release cannot carry, compounded by the inflated self-employment base the tax-compliance adjustment cannot reduce; it is IT-3 in DATA_ISSUES_FOR_TECHNICAL_REPORT.md, and the tool-face exposure is 9.7. Measured by europe/model/selfemp_sic_share.py, which reproduces every shipped surface point it measures exactly. See LIKE_FOR_LIKE_SWEEP.md. Why this note is here at 3 to 4 per cent. Spain's 0.9 per cent does not warrant one, and 3 to 4 sits above that and above several residuals that do carry a note on their own face, so consistency keeps it. The three policy dials are unaffected: their contributions change is identically zero at every point. Spain's self-employed leg is 18.5 per cent above its published figure and reaches 0.9 per cent of a displayed cost at worst; Greece's is 25.0 per cent below and reaches under 1 per cent. Neither carries this note.
